blocks.passage:
Numbers are the language of business. Sales, costs, hours, people — everything is measured.

In English, big numbers can feel tricky at first. 1,000 is "a thousand". 1,000,000 is "a million". Percentages use the word percent, as in "ten percent".

Simple charts tell a story. A line going up means growth. A line going down means decline. A big piece of the pie means a big part. Numbers, then a story — that is the way.

items.q: What does the text call 'the language of business'?
How do you say 1,000,000 in English?
What word do percentages use?
items.why: "Percentages use the word percent, as in 'ten percent'."

items.q: On a chart, what does a line going up mean?
What does the text say is 'the way'?
items.why: "Numbers, then a story — that is the way."

audio.text:
I'm showing the team a simple chart of last month's sales, and I want to do it the right way: show the number, then tell the story. Numbers alone are boring; a story makes them stick.

Here's the chart. The line goes up — that's the first thing your eye sees. Up is good. Up means growth.

Now the number. Sales were up eight percent compared with the same month last year. Eight percent. I'll say it slowly, because it's the main point.

But a number alone doesn't mean much. So here's the story: eight percent growth, and most of it came from our two new Brazilian clients. So the message isn't just 'sales went up' — it's 'the new clients are already paying off'.

See the difference? 'Sales up eight percent' is a number. 'The new clients are already paying off' is a story the team will remember next week.

Always do both: show the number, then tell people what it means. A chart shows; a story sticks.

items.q: What does Harry want to do the right way?
options: Tell a story with no numbers
Show the number, then tell the story
items.why: "show the number, then tell the story."
